title: Thermodynamics
subject: Chemistry
ref: NCERT Chemistry Part I · Unit 5 · pp. 136–167
synopsis:
Thermodynamics answers three questions about any chemical change: how much energy is involved (ΔU, ΔH), will it happen on its own (ΔS, ΔG), and how far will it go (K). The chapter builds this one state function at a time: U → H → S → G.

Tap any branch to go deeper. Every node has its own synopsis and questions.

children.title: Why Thermodynamics?
children.synopsis:
Energy stored in chemical bonds can come out as heat (burning methane or coal), as mechanical work (fuel in an engine) or as electrical energy (a dry cell). These forms of energy can be converted into one another, and thermodynamics is the study of those conversions.

Three ideas fix the scope of the whole chapter:

  • It deals with macroscopic systems: huge numbers of molecules, not a handful.
  • It cares only about the initial and final states. It says nothing about how fast or by what mechanism a change happens. Rate belongs to chemical kinetics.
  • Its laws apply to systems in equilibrium, or moving from one equilibrium state to another. In equilibrium, bulk properties such as p and T do not change with time.

The chapter answers three questions: how much energy a reaction involves, whether it will happen on its own, and how far it will go.
points: Thermodynamics is about macroscopic systems.
It depends on initial and final states only, never on rate or mechanism.
Its laws apply to equilibrium states or changes between them.
traps: Thermodynamics can tell you a reaction is feasible but NOT how fast it goes. Diamond → graphite is thermodynamically favourable yet extremely slow.

questions.q: Which of the following can thermodynamics NOT tell us about a reaction?
o: The rate at which it proceeds
The extent to which it proceeds
questions.e: Thermodynamics looks only at initial and final states. Rate and mechanism belong to chemical kinetics.

questions.q: The laws of thermodynamics are applicable to:
o: Macroscopic systems with a very large number of molecules
questions.e: NCERT stresses that thermodynamics deals with macroscopic (bulk) systems, not microscopic ones.

children.title: 5.1 Thermodynamic Terms
children.synopsis: Before doing any calculation we need a shared vocabulary: system, surroundings, boundary, the types of system, the state of a system, and the central quantity internal energy (U). This section ends with the First Law, ΔU = q + w.

children.title: 5.1.1 System & Surroundings
children.synopsis: The system is the part of the universe we are studying. Everything else is the surroundings. Together they make the universe.

children.title: Universe = System + Surroundings
children.synopsis:
The system is the part of the universe where we make observations. The surroundings are everything else.

In practice, most of the universe is untouched by a reaction in a beaker. So NCERT treats the surroundings as only the part that can interact with the system, usually the space right around it.

Example: A and B react in a beaker. The beaker with the reaction mixture is the system, and the room is the surroundings.
points: Surroundings = the part of the rest of the universe that can interact with the system.
Beaker plus reaction mixture = system; the room = surroundings.

questions.q: For practical purposes in thermodynamics, the surroundings are:
o: The entire universe except the system
That portion of the rest of the universe which can interact with the system
questions.e: Formally the surroundings are everything except the system, but in practice only the region that can interact with the system matters.

children.title: Boundary (Wall)
children.synopsis:
The system is separated from the surroundings by a boundary (wall). The wall can be real (the glass of a beaker) or imaginary (a set of coordinates enclosing a volume of space).

We need a boundary so we can keep track of all matter and energy crossing into or out of the system.

NCERT footnote: if we choose only the reactants as the system, the beaker walls become the boundary.
points: The boundary may be real or imaginary.
Its purpose is to account for every transfer of matter and energy.

questions.q: Which statement about the boundary of a thermodynamic system is correct?
o: It must always be a physical wall
It can be real or imaginary
It never allows energy to pass
It is part of the surroundings only
questions.e: The boundary can be a real wall (beaker) or an imaginary surface defined by coordinates.

children.title: 5.1.2 Types of System
children.synopsis:
Systems are classified by what can cross the boundary: matter, energy, both, or neither.

SystemMatter exchangeEnergy exchangeNCERT example
Open✔✔Reactants in an open beaker
Closed✘✔Reactants in a closed copper/steel vessel
Isolated✘✘Reactants in a thermos flask

children.title: Open System
children.synopsis:
Both energy and matter can be exchanged with the surroundings.

NCERT example: reactants in an open beaker. The boundary is an imaginary surface enclosing the beaker and reactants.

Everyday examples: the human body, a pot of boiling water without a lid.

questions.q: A cup of hot tea kept on a table (without lid) is an example of:
questions.e: Vapour (matter) escapes and heat (energy) is lost, so both matter and energy are exchanged: an open system.

children.title: Closed System
children.synopsis:
No exchange of matter, but energy can be exchanged.

NCERT example: reactants in a closed vessel made of a conducting material such as copper or steel. The walls let heat through but not matter.
traps: The vessel must be conducting. A closed but insulated vessel becomes an isolated system.

questions.q: Reactants sealed in a stoppered steel flask constitute a/an:
questions.e: Matter cannot leave a sealed flask, but steel conducts heat, so energy can be exchanged: a closed system.

children.title: Isolated System
children.synopsis:
Neither energy nor matter is exchanged with the surroundings.

NCERT example: reactants in a thermos flask or any closed, insulated vessel.

Key consequence (used later): with q = 0 and w = 0, an isolated system has ΔU = 0. Its energy is constant.
points: For an isolated system: q = 0, w = 0, so ΔU = 0.

questions.q: For an isolated system, which is always true?
questions.e: No heat or work crosses the boundary, so ΔU = q + w = 0. Entropy can still increase in a spontaneous change.

questions.q: Coffee kept in a perfectly sealed and insulated thermos flask is an example of:
questions.e: Neither matter nor energy can cross the boundary.

children.title: 5.1.3 State of the System
children.synopsis: To calculate anything, we must describe the system before and after a change. Mechanics needs the position and velocity of every particle. Thermodynamics needs only a few average, measurable (macroscopic) properties: p, V, T, n and composition.

children.title: State Variables / State Functions
children.synopsis:
The state of a gas is given by quoting p, V, T, n. These are called state variables or state functions because their values depend only on the current state, not on how the system got there.

Path functions are the opposite: their values depend on the route taken. q and w are path functions (developed in 5.1.4).

State functionsPath functions
p, V, T, U, H, S, Gq (heat), w (work)
points: A state function depends only on the state, not the path.
q and w are path functions, but q + w (= ΔU) is a state function.
traps: q and w are each path dependent, yet their sum ΔU is path independent. This is a favourite assertion–reason question.

questions.q: A thermodynamic state function is a quantity:
o: Whose value is independent of path
Whose value depends on temperature only
questions.e: By definition, a state function depends only on the state of the system, not on how that state was reached.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a state function?
questions.e: Work depends on the path. U, H and S are state functions.

questions.q: Which combination is a state function?
questions.e: q + w = ΔU, which is a state function even though q and w individually are not.

children.title: Minimum Number of Variables
children.synopsis:
You do not need to specify every property to fix the state. Only a certain number can be varied independently, and that number depends on the nature of the system. Once those are fixed, all other properties automatically have definite values.

Example: for a fixed amount of ideal gas, fixing p and T fixes V through pV = nRT.

The state of the surroundings can never be completely specified, and fortunately we never need to.

questions.q: For a fixed amount of an ideal gas, how many of p, V and T must be specified to fix its state?
questions.e: pV = nRT links the three; fixing any two determines the third.

children.title: 5.1.4 Internal Energy as a State Function
children.synopsis: Internal energy (U) is the total energy of the system: chemical, electrical, mechanical, and so on. U changes when heat crosses the boundary, work is done, or matter enters or leaves. This sub-section shows that U is a state function, sets the sign conventions, and arrives at the First Law.

children.title: What is Internal Energy (U)?
children.synopsis:
U is the sum of all forms of energy of the system. It changes when:

  • heat passes into or out of the system,
  • work is done on or by the system,
  • matter enters or leaves the system.

questions.q: The internal energy of a closed system can change by:
questions.e: In general U changes by heat, work or matter transfer. A closed system cannot exchange matter, so only heat and work remain.

children.title: (a) Work: Adiabatic Process & Joule's Experiment
children.synopsis:
Water in a thermos flask (insulated) cannot exchange heat. This is an adiabatic system, its wall is an adiabatic wall, and a change in it is an adiabatic process (q = 0).

Joule (1840–50): doing 1 kJ of work on the water, either by churning it with paddles (mechanical work) or with an immersion rod (electrical work), gave the same temperature rise (state A → state B).

So the same adiabatic work always produces the same change of state, whatever the path. That lets us define U as a quantity fixed by the state:

ΔU = U₂ − U₁ = wad

Therefore U is a state function.

Other familiar state functions are V, p and T. Going from 25 °C to 35 °C gives ΔT = +10 °C whether you heat directly or cool first and then heat. NCERT's analogy: the volume of water in a pond changes by the same amount whether it is filled by rain, a tubewell or both.
points: Adiabatic: no heat transfer (q = 0).
ΔU = w_ad shows U is a state function.

questions.q: For a process to occur under adiabatic conditions, the correct condition is:
questions.e: Adiabatic means no heat exchange with the surroundings, so q = 0.

questions.q: Joule's experiments with paddle-churning and electrical heating of water in an insulated vessel showed that:
o: Mechanical work produces more heat than electrical work
A given amount of adiabatic work produces the same change of state regardless of how it is done
Internal energy depends on the path
questions.e: Equal amounts of adiabatic work by different routes gave the same temperature rise, so U is a state function.

children.title: Sign Convention (IUPAC)
children.synopsis:
The IUPAC convention is 'positive = added to the system':

QuantityPositive (+)Negative (−)
wWork done on the system (U rises)Work done by the system (U falls)
qHeat absorbed by the systemHeat released to the surroundings

NCERT footnote: the old convention (still used in many physics books) gave work done on the system a negative sign, so the First Law appears there as ΔU = q − w. Chemistry uses IUPAC, ΔU = q + w.
traps: Physics books may write ΔU = q − W (W = work done BY the gas). Do not mix conventions within one problem.

questions.q: According to the IUPAC convention, work done on the system is:
questions.e: Energy added to the system (work done on it) is positive.

questions.q: A system absorbs 701 J of heat and does 394 J of work. ΔU of the system is:
questions.e: q = +701 J and w = −394 J (work done by the system). ΔU = 701 − 394 = +307 J.

children.title: (b) Heat
children.synopsis:
U can also change by heat (q) alone: an energy exchange caused by a temperature difference.

Put water at TA in a thermally conducting (e.g. copper) container inside a large reservoir at TB. The heat absorbed is measured from TB − TA.

With no work done (constant volume):

ΔU = q

q is positive when heat flows into the system and negative when it flows out.

questions.q: If no work is done on or by a system at constant volume, the change in internal energy equals:
questions.e: With w = 0, ΔU = q.

children.title: (c) First Law of Thermodynamics
children.synopsis:
In general a change happens through both heat and work:

ΔU = q + w (Eq. 5.1)

q and w each depend on how the change is carried out, but their sum depends only on the initial and final states.

For an isolated system, q = 0 and w = 0, so ΔU = 0. This is the First Law:

The energy of an isolated system is constant.

In other words, it is the law of conservation of energy: energy can neither be created nor destroyed.

NCERT Problem 5.1 pattern:

  • No heat, work w done on the system → ΔU = wad (adiabatic wall)
  • No work, heat q removed → ΔU = −q (thermally conducting wall)
  • Work w done by the system, heat q supplied → ΔU = q − w (closed system)

questions.q: The mathematical statement of the first law of thermodynamics (IUPAC convention) is:
questions.e: With the IUPAC sign convention, ΔU = q + w.

questions.q: A gas does 200 J of work on the surroundings while 300 J of heat is removed from it. ΔU is:
questions.e: w = −200 J and q = −300 J, so ΔU = −500 J.

questions.q: No work is done on a system but heat q is taken out of it. The system has:
questions.e: Heat can leave only through thermally conducting walls. ΔU = −q (NCERT Problem 5.1 ii).

children.title: Absolute U Cannot Be Measured
children.synopsis: Energy differs from a mechanical property like volume. We can state an exact absolute value of V for a state, but not the absolute value of U. Only changes, ΔU, can be measured.

questions.q: Which of the following can be measured absolutely for a system in a given state?
questions.e: Volume has an absolute value. For U, H and G only changes can be measured.

children.title: 5.2 Applications: Work & Enthalpy
children.synopsis: Many reactions produce gases that can push a piston (work) or release heat. This section puts numbers on both. It derives the work formulas for different processes, introduces the new state function enthalpy (H), separates extensive and intensive properties, and defines heat capacity along with Cp − CV = R.

children.title: 5.2.1 Work (Pressure–Volume Work)
children.synopsis: Only mechanical (pressure–volume) work is considered. Picture one mole of ideal gas in a cylinder with a frictionless piston. The work depends on how the external pressure changes during the process.

children.title: Single-step Work: w = −pₑₓΔV
children.synopsis:
A constant external pressure pex compresses the gas in one step. The piston (area A) moves a distance l, so ΔV = l × A = Vf − Vi.

Force = pex · A, so work = force × distance = pex · A · l. Adding the sign:

w = −pexΔV = −pex(Vf − Vi) (Eq. 5.2)

The minus sign makes the convention work out. In compression ΔV is negative, so w comes out positive (work done on the system). In expansion ΔV is positive, so w is negative.

On a p–V graph, the work equals the shaded rectangle under the constant pex line.
traps: Always use EXTERNAL pressure, not gas pressure, for irreversible work.

questions.q: An ideal gas expands from 2 L to 5 L against a constant external pressure of 1 atm. The work done (1 L atm = 101.3 J) is about:
questions.e: w = −p_ex ΔV = −1 × (5 − 2) = −3 L atm ≈ −304 J. It is negative because the gas does work on the surroundings.

questions.q: During compression of a gas, the sign of work (IUPAC) is positive because:
o: ΔV is negative, and w = −p_ex ΔV
questions.e: In compression V_f < V_i, so ΔV < 0 and w = −p_ex ΔV > 0.

children.title: Multi-step & Reversible Processes
children.synopsis:
Finite steps: if pex changes in several steps, total work = −Σ pΔV, a staircase of rectangles on the p–V graph.

Infinite steps: if pex is always only infinitesimally greater than the gas pressure (pex = pin + dp for compression, pin − dp for expansion), then

w = −∫ pex dV (Eq. 5.3)

Such a process is reversible. At any moment it could be reversed by an infinitesimal change. It proceeds infinitely slowly through a series of equilibrium states, with the system and surroundings always in near-equilibrium.

All other processes are irreversible.
points: Reversible: infinitely slow, a series of equilibrium states, reversible by an infinitesimal change.
On a p–V graph, reversible compression needs the least work and reversible expansion gives the most work.

questions.q: A reversible process is one which:
o: Proceeds infinitely slowly through a series of equilibrium states
Can be reversed only by a large change
questions.e: NCERT: a reversible process proceeds infinitely slowly through equilibrium states and can be reversed by an infinitesimal change.

questions.q: For the same initial and final volumes, the magnitude of work done BY a gas on isothermal expansion is maximum when the expansion is:
questions.e: In reversible expansion, p_ex tracks the gas pressure, giving the largest area under the p–V curve.

children.title: Isothermal Reversible Work
children.synopsis:
Under reversible conditions pex = pin ± dp. Since dp·dV is negligible, we can replace pex with the gas pressure p:

wrev = −∫ p dV (Eq. 5.4)

For n mol of ideal gas, p = nRT/V. At constant T (isothermal):

wrev = −nRT ln(Vf/Vi) = −2.303 nRT log(Vf/Vi) (Eq. 5.5)

Since p1V1 = p2V2 at constant T, you can also write Vf/Vi = pi/pf.

questions.q: 2 mol of an ideal gas expand isothermally and reversibly at 300 K from 10 L to 100 L. Work done is about (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹):
In the expression w_rev = −2.303 nRT log(V_f/V_i), the ratio V_f/V_i can be replaced (isothermal ideal gas) by:
questions.e: Boyle's law: p_i V_i = p_f V_f, so V_f/V_i = p_i/p_f.

children.title: Free Expansion
children.synopsis:
Expansion of a gas into vacuum (pex = 0) is free expansion. No work is done, whether the process is reversible or irreversible.

For an ideal gas expanding isothermally into vacuum, Joule found experimentally that q = 0 as well. So ΔU = 0.

NCERT Problem 5.2: 2 L of gas at 10 atm expands isothermally into vacuum to 10 L. Then q = −w = 0 × 8 = 0: no work and no heat.
points: Free expansion: p_ex = 0, so w = 0.
Ideal gas, isothermal free expansion: q = 0, w = 0, ΔU = 0.

questions.q: An ideal gas expands isothermally into vacuum. Which is correct?
questions.e: Against zero external pressure, w = 0. For an ideal gas at constant T, ΔU = 0, so q = 0 too.

children.title: q and w for Different Processes
children.synopsis:
Put w = −pexΔV into the First Law: ΔU = q − pexΔV.

ProcessResult
Constant volume (ΔV = 0)ΔU = qV
Isothermal irreversible (ideal gas, ΔU = 0)q = −w = pex(Vf − Vi)
Isothermal reversible (ideal gas)q = −w = 2.303 nRT log(Vf/Vi)
Adiabaticq = 0, ΔU = wad

NCERT trio for one expansion (2 L → 10 L, 25 °C):

  • Into vacuum: q = 0
  • Against 1 atm: q = 8 L atm
  • Reversible, 1 mol: q ≈ 39.4 L atm

The same initial and final states give different q and w on different paths, a direct demonstration that q and w are path functions.

questions.q: For an isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, which statement is correct?
questions.e: For an ideal gas, U depends only on T. Isothermal means ΔU = 0, so q = −w.

questions.q: Heat absorbed at constant volume equals:
questions.e: At constant volume no pV work is done, so ΔU = q_V.

children.title: 5.2.2 Enthalpy (H)
children.synopsis: Most reactions run at constant pressure (open flasks, test tubes), not constant volume. So we define a state function whose change equals the heat at constant pressure: enthalpy, H = U + pV. This sub-topic also covers extensive vs intensive properties, heat capacity, and Cp − CV = R.

children.title: (a) H = U + pV and ΔH = q(p)
children.synopsis:
At constant pressure: ΔU = qp − pΔV. Rearranging gives qp = (U2 + pV2) − (U1 + pV1). This motivates:

H = U + pV (Eq. 5.7) so qp = ΔH

The word comes from the Greek enthalpien, 'to warm' or 'heat content'.

  • H depends on U, p and V, which are all state functions, so H is a state function.
  • Therefore qp is path-independent, even though q in general is not.
  • At constant p: ΔH = ΔU + pΔV (Eq. 5.8).
  • At constant V: ΔH = ΔU = qV.

Sign: ΔH is negative for exothermic reactions (heat released) and positive for endothermic reactions (heat absorbed).
traps: q is path-dependent in general, but q_p (= ΔH) and q_V (= ΔU) are path-independent.

questions.q: Heat absorbed by a system at constant pressure is equal to:
questions.e: By definition, ΔH = q_p.

questions.q: For an exothermic reaction:
questions.e: Exothermic reactions release heat, so ΔH is negative.

questions.q: Which statement is correct?
o: q_p is path-independent because it equals ΔH
questions.e: H is a state function, so ΔH, and hence q_p, does not depend on path.

children.title: ΔH = ΔU + Δn(g)RT
children.synopsis:
For solids and liquids, the volume change is tiny, so ΔH ≈ ΔU. With gases the difference matters.

At constant p and T, pVA = nART and pVB = nBRT, so pΔV = ΔngRT. This gives:

ΔH = ΔU + ΔngRT (Eq. 5.10)

Δng = moles of gaseous products − moles of gaseous reactants. Ignore solids and liquids.

ΔngRelation
> 0ΔH > ΔU
= 0ΔH = ΔU
< 0ΔH < ΔU

NCERT Problem 5.5: vaporising 1 mol of water at 100 °C, ΔH = 41 kJ mol⁻¹ and Δng = 1. So ΔU = 41 − (8.3 × 373 × 10⁻³) ≈ 37.9 kJ mol⁻¹.
traps: Count only GASEOUS species for Δn_g. In CH₄ combustion water is liquid, so Δn_g = 1 − 3 = −2.
Use R in kJ (8.314 × 10⁻³ kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) when ΔH is in kJ.

questions.q: For CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), ΔU = −X kJ mol⁻¹. Then ΔH is:
questions.e: Δn_g = 1 − 3 = −2, so ΔH = ΔU − 2RT, which is less than ΔU.

questions.q: For which reaction is ΔH = ΔU?
questions.e: For H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl, Δn_g = 2 − 2 = 0, so ΔH = ΔU.

questions.q: ΔvapH of water at 373 K is 40.7 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔvapU (water vapour as ideal gas) is about:
For C₃H₈(g) + 5O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(l) at 298 K, Δn_g is:
questions.e: Gaseous products 3, gaseous reactants 6, so Δn_g = −3. Liquid water is not counted.

children.title: (b) Extensive & Intensive Properties
children.synopsis:
Extensive: the value depends on the amount of matter. Examples: mass, volume, internal energy, enthalpy, heat capacity (also entropy and Gibbs energy).

Intensive: the value does not depend on amount. Examples: temperature, pressure, density.

Molar property χm = χ/n, an extensive property per mole. It is intensive. Examples: molar volume Vm and molar heat capacity Cm.

NCERT test (Fig 5.6): split a gas (V, T) in half with a partition. Each half has volume V/2 but the same T. So V is extensive and T is intensive.
points: Ratio of two extensive properties = intensive (density = m/V; C_m = C/n).
G is extensive (stated in 5.6 c).
traps: Heat capacity is EXTENSIVE, but specific heat and molar heat capacity are INTENSIVE.

questions.q: Which of the following is an intensive property?
questions.e: Molar heat capacity = C/n, the ratio of two extensive quantities, so it is intensive.

questions.q: Which set contains only extensive properties?
questions.e: Mass, volume and enthalpy all scale with the amount of substance.

children.title: (c) Heat Capacity
children.synopsis:
Heat absorbed shows up as a temperature rise: q = C ΔT, where C is the heat capacity. Its magnitude depends on the size, composition and nature of the system.

  • Large C, small temperature rise for a given heat. Water has a large heat capacity.
  • Molar heat capacity Cm = C/n: heat to raise 1 mol by 1 °C (1 K).
  • Specific heat (capacity) c: heat to raise unit mass by 1 °C (1 K).

q = c × m × ΔT = C ΔT (Eq. 5.11)

questions.q: Heat needed to raise the temperature of 60.0 g of Al from 35 °C to 55 °C (molar heat capacity 24 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, M = 27 g mol⁻¹) is about:
A substance with a large heat capacity will show:
o: A large temperature rise for a given heat input
A small temperature rise for a given heat input
questions.e: q = CΔT, so for fixed q, a larger C gives a smaller ΔT.

children.title: (d) Cp − Cv = R (Ideal Gas)
children.synopsis:
qV = CVΔT = ΔU and qp = CpΔT = ΔH.

For 1 mol of ideal gas, ΔH = ΔU + Δ(pV) = ΔU + Δ(RT) = ΔU + RΔT. Substituting:

CpΔT = CVΔT + RΔT ⟹ Cp − CV = R (Eq. 5.13)

So Cp > CV always. At constant pressure, part of the heat goes into expansion work.

Useful extra (from the NCERT box in 5.5): for a monoatomic gas, CV = 3/2 R and Cp = 5/2 R.

questions.q: For one mole of an ideal gas, Cp − Cv equals:
questions.e: From ΔH = ΔU + RΔT for 1 mol of ideal gas, Cp − Cv = R.

questions.q: Why is Cp greater than Cv for a gas?
o: At constant pressure, part of the heat is used to do expansion work
At constant volume, heat is lost
questions.e: At constant p, the gas expands and does work, so more heat is needed for the same ΔT.

children.title: 5.3 Measuring ΔU and ΔH: Calorimetry
children.synopsis: Calorimetry measures heat changes. The process runs in a calorimeter immersed in a known volume of liquid. Knowing the heat capacities of the liquid and the calorimeter, the measured temperature change gives the heat. There are two set-ups: constant volume (gives ΔU) and constant pressure (gives ΔH).

children.title: (a) ΔU: Bomb Calorimeter
children.synopsis:
A sealed steel vessel (the bomb) sits in a water bath, so no heat is lost to the surroundings. The substance burns in pure dioxygen inside the bomb. The heat released passes into the water, and its temperature is monitored.

  • The bomb is sealed, so volume is constant. No work is done, even for reactions involving gases (ΔV = 0).
  • The heat measured is qV = ΔU. It comes from ΔT and the known heat capacity of the calorimeter (q = CΔT).

questions.q: A bomb calorimeter measures:
questions.e: The bomb is sealed and rigid (ΔV = 0), so the heat measured is q_V = ΔU.

questions.q: Why is no work done in a bomb calorimeter even when gases are produced?
o: The volume of the sealed bomb is constant
questions.e: w = −pΔV and ΔV = 0 in the sealed steel bomb.

children.title: (b) ΔH: Constant-pressure Calorimeter
children.synopsis:
Heat changes at constant (atmospheric) pressure are measured in an open calorimeter (Fig 5.8). Since ΔH = qp, the heat measured is the heat of reaction, or enthalpy of reaction, ΔrH.

  • Exothermic: heat evolved, qp < 0, ΔrH < 0
  • Endothermic: heat absorbed, qp > 0, ΔrH > 0

questions.q: The heat absorbed or evolved at constant pressure in a calorimeter is called:
questions.e: q_p = Δ_rH, the enthalpy (heat) of reaction.

children.title: Worked: Burning Graphite in a Bomb
children.synopsis:
1 g of graphite burns in a bomb calorimeter (CV = 20.7 kJ K⁻¹), and the temperature rises from 298 K to 299 K.

  1. Heat gained by the calorimeter = 20.7 × 1 = 20.7 kJ. The reaction lost the same amount, so q = −20.7 kJ per gram.
  2. Per mole (12 g): ΔU = 12 × (−20.7) = −2.48 × 10² kJ mol⁻¹.
  3. C(s) + O2(g) → CO2(g) has Δng = 1 − 1 = 0, so ΔH = ΔU.

NCERT erratum: the text writes ΔU for 1 g as '−20.7 kJ K⁻¹'. The correct unit is kJ (it is an energy, not a heat capacity).

questions.q: A reaction in a bomb calorimeter (heat capacity 10.0 kJ K⁻¹) raises the temperature by 2.0 K. q for the reaction is:
questions.e: The calorimeter gains CΔT = 20 kJ. The reaction lost it, so q = −20 kJ (exothermic).

questions.q: For C(graphite) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), the relation between ΔH and ΔU is:
questions.e: Δn_g = 1 − 1 = 0, so ΔH = ΔU.

children.title: 5.4 Reaction Enthalpy (ΔᵣH)
children.synopsis:
The enthalpy change that accompanies a reaction is the reaction enthalpy, ΔrH:

ΔrH = Σ ai H(products) − Σ bi H(reactants) (Eq. 5.14)

Industry needs it to plan heating or cooling, and it is also needed for the temperature dependence of K. This section covers standard states, phase changes, enthalpy of formation, thermochemical equations and Hess's law.

children.title: ΔᵣH = ΣH(products) − ΣH(reactants)
children.synopsis:
The ai and bi are the stoichiometric coefficients from the balanced equation, and Hm is the molar enthalpy.

Example: CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → CO2(g) + 2H2O(l)

ΔrH = [Hm(CO2) + 2Hm(H2O,l)] − [Hm(CH4) + 2Hm(O2)]

Uses: planning the heating or cooling needed to keep an industrial reaction at constant temperature, and calculating how the equilibrium constant changes with temperature.

questions.q: Knowledge of Δ_rH is needed for all EXCEPT:
o: Planning heating/cooling of an industrial reaction
Temperature dependence of the equilibrium constant
Predicting the rate constant of a reaction
questions.e: Rate constants belong to chemical kinetics. NCERT lists the other uses.

children.title: (a) Standard Enthalpy & Standard State
children.synopsis:
Enthalpy depends on conditions, so we fix standard ones.

Standard enthalpy of reaction (ΔrH°): the enthalpy change when all participants are in their standard states.

Standard state of a substance at a given temperature: its pure form at 1 bar.

  • Liquid ethanol at 298 K: pure liquid ethanol at 1 bar.
  • Solid iron at 500 K: pure iron at 1 bar.

Data are usually quoted at 298 K. Standard conditions are shown by the superscript °.
traps: The standard state specifies PRESSURE (1 bar), not temperature. A standard state can exist at any temperature; 298 K is just the usual choice.

questions.q: The standard state of a substance at a specified temperature is:
o: Its pure form at 1 atm and 273 K
Its most stable form at 298 K only
questions.e: NCERT: the standard state is the pure form at 1 bar at the specified temperature.

children.title: (b) Enthalpy of Phase Transformations
children.synopsis:
Phase changes happen at constant temperature (and pressure), and they still involve energy.

TermProcess (1 mol, standard state)Example
ΔfusH°solid → liquidIce: 6.00 kJ mol⁻¹ at 273 K
ΔvapH°liquid → vapour (at Tb, 1 bar)Water: +40.79 kJ mol⁻¹
ΔsubH°solid → vapour directlyDry ice: 25.2 kJ mol⁻¹ at 195 K; naphthalene: 73.0 kJ mol⁻¹
  • Melting, vaporisation and sublimation are all endothermic, so these enthalpies are positive. The reverse processes (freezing, condensation) release the same amount.
  • The magnitude depends on intermolecular forces. Water has strong H-bonds and acetone weaker dipole–dipole forces, so acetone needs less heat per mole to vaporise.
  • Since the paths are equivalent (Hess), ΔsubH = ΔfusH + ΔvapH at the same temperature.

Problem 5.7: 18 g of water on a swimmer at 298 K (ΔvapH = 44.01 kJ mol⁻¹) needs 44.01 kJ. Then ΔvapU = 44.01 − RT = 44.01 − 2.48 = 41.53 kJ.

Problem 5.8: 1 mol of water at 100 °C → ice at 0 °C. ΔH = −(18 × 4.2 × 100) J − 6.00 kJ = −7.56 − 6.00 = −13.56 kJ mol⁻¹. The volume change is negligible, so ΔU ≈ ΔH.

questions.q: Which is true for all enthalpies of fusion and vaporisation?
o: They are zero at the transition temperature
They are equal for all substances
questions.e: Melting and vaporising need heat (endothermic), so these enthalpies are positive.

questions.q: Acetone needs less heat per mole than water to vaporise because:
o: Acetone has a higher molar mass
Water has strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds
questions.e: Strong H-bonding in water holds the molecules tightly. Acetone has only weaker dipole–dipole forces.

questions.q: If ΔfusH = 6.0 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔvapH = 45.0 kJ mol⁻¹ for a substance at the same temperature, its ΔsubH is:
questions.e: Solid → vapour = solid → liquid → vapour, so ΔsubH = 6.0 + 45.0 = 51.0 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.q: During melting of ice at 273 K and 1 atm, the temperature:
questions.e: Phase changes take place at constant temperature; the heat absorbed is latent heat.

children.title: (c) Standard Enthalpy of Formation
children.synopsis:
ΔfH°: the standard enthalpy change for forming one mole of a compound from its elements in their most stable states (reference states).

Reference state of an element is its most stable form at 25 °C and 1 bar: H2(g), O2(g), C(graphite), S(rhombic).

NCERT examples: ΔfH° of H2O(l) = −285.8, CH4(g) = −74.81, C2H5OH(l) = −277.7 kJ mol⁻¹.

Convention: ΔfH° of an element in its reference state = 0.

These are NOT formation enthalpies:

  • CaO(s) + CO2(g) → CaCO3(s), ΔrH = −178.3 kJ: formed from compounds, not elements.
  • H2(g) + Br2(l) → 2HBr(g): two moles formed. Halve it to get ΔfH°(HBr) = −36.4 kJ mol⁻¹.

NCERT erratum: for H₂ + Br₂ → 2HBr the text prints ΔrH° = −178.3 kJ mol⁻¹ (copied from the CaCO₃ line). The consistent value is 2 × (−36.4) = −72.8 kJ mol⁻¹.
points: ΔfH° of an element in its most stable form is 0 (e.g. O₂(g), C(graphite)).
ΔfH° of C(diamond) or O₃(g) is NOT zero, because they are not reference states.
traps: ΔfH°(Br₂, l) = 0 but ΔfH°(Br₂, g) ≠ 0, because liquid is bromine's reference state.

questions.q: The enthalpies of all elements in their standard (reference) states are:
questions.e: By convention ΔfH° = 0 for every element in its most stable state at 1 bar.

questions.q: For which substance is ΔfH° NOT zero?
questions.e: Diamond is not carbon's reference state; graphite is.

questions.q: Which equation represents the standard enthalpy of formation?
questions.e: It forms 1 mol of HBr from its elements in their reference states. The others start from compounds, make 2 mol, or use diamond.

questions.q: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g), ΔrH° = −92.4 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔfH° of NH₃(g) is:
questions.e: The equation makes 2 mol of NH₃, so ΔfH° = −92.4/2 = −46.2 kJ mol⁻¹.

children.title: Using ΔfH° to Find ΔᵣH°
children.synopsis:
ΔrH° = Σ ai ΔfH°(products) − Σ bi ΔfH°(reactants) (Eq. 5.15)

NCERT example: CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g)

ΔrH° = (−635.1) + (−393.5) − (−1206.9) = +178.3 kJ mol⁻¹. The reaction is endothermic, so limestone must be heated to make lime.

Recipe: products minus reactants, each multiplied by its coefficient; elements count as zero.

questions.q: ΔfH° values (kJ mol⁻¹): CO(g) = −110, CO₂(g) = −393, N₂O(g) = 81, N₂O₄(g) = 9.7. ΔrH for N₂O₄(g) + 3CO(g) → N₂O(g) + 3CO₂(g) is:
Given ΔfH°: Fe₂O₃(s) = −824.2, H₂O(l) = −285.83 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔrH° for Fe₂O₃(s) + 3H₂(g) → 2Fe(s) + 3H₂O(l) is about:

children.title: (d) Thermochemical Equations
children.synopsis:
A thermochemical equation is a balanced equation plus its ΔrH, with the physical state (and allotropic form) of every substance written in.

Example: C2H5OH(l) + 3O2(g) → 2CO2(g) + 3H2O(l); ΔrH° = −1367 kJ mol⁻¹

Three conventions:

  1. Coefficients mean moles, never molecules.
  2. ΔrH° refers to the moles as written, and its unit is kJ mol⁻¹, meaning per mole of reaction. Halve the equation and you halve ΔH (−33.3 becomes −16.6 kJ for the Fe2O3 example). So enthalpy is extensive.
  3. Reverse the equation and the sign of ΔH flips. N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3 is −91.8 kJ; 2NH3 → N2 + 3H2 is +91.8 kJ.

questions.q: If ΔH for A → B is −x kJ, then ΔH for 2B → 2A is:
questions.e: Reversing flips the sign (+x) and doubling doubles the value: +2x kJ.

questions.q: In a thermochemical equation, the stoichiometric coefficients represent:
questions.e: NCERT convention 1: coefficients are moles, never molecules.

questions.q: Heat released on forming 35.2 g of CO₂ from carbon (ΔcH of C = −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹) is:

children.title: (e) Hess's Law of Constant Heat Summation
children.synopsis:
Enthalpy is a state function, so ΔH for a reaction is the same whether it happens in one step or many.

If a reaction takes place in several steps, its standard reaction enthalpy is the sum of the standard enthalpies of the intermediate reactions (at the same temperature).

ΔrH = ΔrH1 + ΔrH2 + ΔrH3 + … (Eq. 5.16)

Why we need it: burning carbon always gives some CO2 along with CO, so ΔrH for C → CO cannot be measured directly.

  1. C(graphite) + O2 → CO2; ΔH = −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹
  2. CO + ½O2 → CO2; ΔH = −283.0 kJ mol⁻¹
  3. Reverse (2): CO2 → CO + ½O2; ΔH = +283.0
  4. Add (1) and (3): C + ½O2 → CO; ΔH = −110.5 kJ mol⁻¹

Toolkit: equations can be added, subtracted, reversed (flip the sign) and multiplied (scale ΔH), exactly like algebra.

questions.q: Hess's law is a direct consequence of the fact that:
questions.e: ΔH depends only on the initial and final states, so it is the same for any route.

questions.q: C(s) + O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −393.5 kJ; CO + ½O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −283.0 kJ. ΔH for C(s) + ½O₂ → CO is:
Why can ΔH for C(graphite) + ½O₂ → CO not be measured directly?
o: Some CO₂ is always formed along with CO
questions.e: NCERT: some CO₂ always forms, so direct measurement is impossible; Hess's law is used instead.

questions.q: Given A → B, ΔH = +20 kJ; B → C, ΔH = −50 kJ; C → D, ΔH = +10 kJ. ΔH for D → A is:

children.title: 5.5 Enthalpies for Different Types of Reactions
children.synopsis:
Special reactions get their own named enthalpies: combustion, atomization, bond enthalpy, lattice enthalpy, solution and dilution. Each is defined per mole, under standard conditions.

SymbolNameSign
ΔcHCombustionAlways −
ΔaHAtomizationAlways +
ΔbondHBond (dissociation / mean)+ (breaking)
ΔlatticeHLattice (solid → gaseous ions)+
ΔsolHSolution+ or −
ΔdilHDilution+ or −

children.title: (a) Enthalpy of Combustion (ΔcH°)
children.synopsis:
ΔcH°: the enthalpy change per mole of a substance when it burns completely, with all reactants and products in their standard states. Combustion is always exothermic.

  • Butane (cooking gas): C4H10(g) + 13/2 O2 → 4CO2 + 5H2O(l); ΔcH = −2658 kJ mol⁻¹
  • Glucose: ΔcH = −2802 kJ mol⁻¹. Our body extracts energy from food through the same overall process, by a series of enzyme-catalysed steps.

Problem 5.9 (benzene): ΔcH(C6H6, l) = −3267 kJ mol⁻¹. Using ΔfH(CO2) = −393.5 and ΔfH(H2O) = −285.83:

ΔfH(C6H6) = 6(−393.5) + 3(−285.83) − (−3267) = +48.51 kJ mol⁻¹

NCERT erratum: the final line of Problem 5.9 prints −48.51 kJ mol⁻¹. The arithmetic gives +48.51 kJ mol⁻¹ (benzene has a positive enthalpy of formation): −3218.49 + 3267.0 = +48.51.

Shortcut: ΔfH(compound) = Σ ΔcH(elements) − ΔcH(compound).

questions.q: ΔcH of ethane, graphite and H₂ are −1560, −393.5 and −285.8 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔfH of C₂H₆(g) is about:
ΔcH of methane, graphite and H₂ are −890.3, −393.5 and −285.8 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔfH of CH₄(g) is:
Enthalpy of combustion is always:
questions.e: Combustion releases heat, so ΔcH < 0.

children.title: (b) Enthalpy of Atomization (ΔₐH°)
children.synopsis:
ΔaH°: the enthalpy change on breaking one mole of a substance completely into gaseous atoms.

  • H2(g) → 2H(g); ΔaH = 435.0 kJ mol⁻¹. For diatomic molecules this also equals the bond dissociation enthalpy.
  • CH4(g) → C(g) + 4H(g); ΔaH = 1665 kJ mol⁻¹
  • Na(s) → Na(g); ΔaH = 108.4 kJ mol⁻¹. For a metal, atomization = sublimation.

The products are always only gaseous atoms.

questions.q: For sodium metal, the enthalpy of atomization is the same as its:
questions.e: Na(s) → Na(g) is both atomization and sublimation.

questions.q: For which species is the enthalpy of atomization equal to its bond dissociation enthalpy?
questions.e: For diatomic molecules, breaking the one bond gives atoms directly.

children.title: (c) Bond Enthalpy (ΔbondH°)
children.synopsis: Breaking bonds needs energy and making bonds releases energy. Two terms are used: bond dissociation enthalpy and mean bond enthalpy.

children.title: Bond Dissociation Enthalpy (Diatomic)
children.synopsis:
The enthalpy change when one mole of covalent bonds of a gaseous covalent compound is broken to give products in the gas phase.

  • H2(g) → 2H(g); ΔH–HH = 435.0 kJ mol⁻¹
  • Cl2(g) → 2Cl(g); 242 kJ mol⁻¹
  • O2(g) → 2O(g); 428 kJ mol⁻¹

For diatomic molecules this equals the enthalpy of atomization.

questions.q: Bond dissociation enthalpy refers to breaking one mole of bonds of a compound in which state?
questions.e: Both reactant and products must be gaseous.

children.title: Mean Bond Enthalpy (Polyatomic)
children.synopsis:
In CH4 the four C–H bonds are identical, yet breaking them one after another needs different energies:

StepΔbondH (kJ mol⁻¹)
CH4 → CH3 + H427
CH3 → CH2 + H439
CH2 → CH + H452
CH → C + H347
Total (= ΔaH)1665

So we use the mean bond enthalpy: ΔC–HH = ¼ × 1665 = 416 kJ mol⁻¹.

Mean C–H enthalpy varies slightly from compound to compound (CH3CH2Cl, CH3NO2…) but not a great deal. Table 5.3 lists mean values, e.g. H–H 435.8, C–C 347, C=C 611, C≡C 837, N≡N 946, O=O 498 kJ mol⁻¹.
points: Mean bond enthalpy = ΔaH ÷ number of equivalent bonds.

questions.q: ΔaH of NH₃(g) is 1171 kJ mol⁻¹. The mean N–H bond enthalpy is about:
questions.e: There are 3 N–H bonds, so 1171 ÷ 3 ≈ 390 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.q: The successive C–H bond dissociation enthalpies in CH₄ are different because:
o: The four C–H bonds have different lengths
The chemical environment changes after each H is removed
questions.e: Each fragment (CH₃, CH₂, CH) is a different species, so the energy to remove the next H differs, even though all bonds in CH₄ are identical.

children.title: ΔᵣH from Bond Enthalpies
children.synopsis:
For gas-phase reactions:

ΔrH° = Σ bond enthalpies(reactants) − Σ bond enthalpies(products) (Eq. 5.17)

The net change is the energy to break all reactant bonds minus the energy to break all product bonds (which is the energy released forming them).

  • Most useful when ΔfH values are not available.
  • It is approximate (mean values) and valid only when all species are gaseous.

Footnote: written with bond formation enthalpies, the order flips: products − reactants.
traps: For bond enthalpies it is REACTANTS − PRODUCTS, the opposite of the ΔfH formula (products − reactants).

questions.q: Using bond enthalpies H–H = 435.8, Cl–Cl = 243, H–Cl = 431 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔrH for H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g) is about:
The relation ΔrH = ΣBE(reactants) − ΣBE(products) is strictly applicable when:
o: All species are in the solid state
All species are in the gaseous state
questions.e: Bond enthalpies are defined for gaseous molecules, so the relation holds only for gas-phase reactions.

children.title: (d) Lattice Enthalpy & Born–Haber Cycle
children.synopsis:
Lattice enthalpy: the enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic compound dissociates into its gaseous ions.

Na⁺Cl⁻(s) → Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g); ΔlatticeH° = +788 kJ mol⁻¹

It cannot be measured directly, so we use an enthalpy cycle, the Born–Haber cycle. For NaCl:

  1. Na(s) → Na(g): sublimation, +108.4
  2. Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻: ionization, +496
  3. ½Cl2(g) → Cl(g): half the bond enthalpy, +121
  4. Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g): electron gain, −348.6
  5. Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g) → NaCl(s): −ΔlatticeH

The sum around a closed cycle is zero (Hess). With ΔfH(NaCl) = −411.2:

ΔlatticeH = 411.2 + 108.4 + 121 + 496 − 348.6 = +788 kJ

ΔUlattice is smaller by 2RT (Δng = 2), which gives +783 kJ mol⁻¹.
formulas: ΔlatticeH = −ΔfH + ΔsubH + ½ΔbondH + ΔiH + ΔegH (NaCl type)

questions.q: Lattice enthalpy of an ionic compound is defined as the enthalpy change when one mole of it:
questions.e: NCERT: solid → gaseous ions; it is positive (endothermic).

questions.q: The Born–Haber cycle is an application of:
questions.e: The enthalpy changes round a closed cycle add to zero because H is a state function (Hess's law).

questions.q: Lattice enthalpy is determined using the Born–Haber cycle because:
o: It cannot be determined directly by experiment
It is zero for all solids
questions.e: NCERT: lattice enthalpies cannot be measured directly, so an indirect cycle is used.

children.title: Box: Ionization Energy vs Ionization Enthalpy
children.synopsis:
Ionization energy and electron affinity are defined at absolute zero. At any other temperature T, the heat capacities of reactants and products must be included.

For each gaseous species, Cp = 5/2 R (CV = 3/2 R). This gives:

  • Ionization: ΔrCp = +5/2 R, so ΔiH = E0 + 5/2 RT
  • Electron gain: ΔrCp = −5/2 R, so ΔegH = −A − 5/2 RT

That is why the modern terms are ionization enthalpy and electron gain enthalpy (Unit 3).

questions.q: Ionization enthalpy (ΔiH) at temperature T is related to ionization energy (E₀) by:
questions.e: From the NCERT box: Δ_rC_p = +5/2 R for ionization, so ΔiH = E₀ + 5/2 RT.

children.title: (e) Enthalpy of Solution (ΔsolH°)
children.synopsis:
ΔsolH: the enthalpy change when one mole of a substance dissolves in a specified amount of solvent. At infinite dilution, interactions between the dissolved particles are negligible.

When an ionic solid dissolves, two things happen: the ions leave the lattice (needs ΔlatticeH) and they get hydrated (releases ΔhydH).

ΔsolH° = ΔlatticeH° + ΔhydH°

NaCl: +788 + (−784) = +4 kJ mol⁻¹, very little heat change.

  • For most ionic compounds ΔsolH is positive (endothermic), so solubility rises with temperature.
  • A very high lattice enthalpy can stop dissolution altogether. NCERT asks why fluorides are often less soluble than chlorides: small F⁻ makes the lattice enthalpy very high.

questions.q: For a salt, ΔlatticeH = +700 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔhydH = −720 kJ mol⁻¹. Its ΔsolH is:
questions.e: ΔsolH = 700 + (−720) = −20 kJ mol⁻¹ (exothermic dissolution).

questions.q: For most ionic compounds, solubility in water increases with temperature because:
questions.e: NCERT: dissolution is usually endothermic, so higher T favours it.

children.title: (f) Enthalpy of Dilution
children.synopsis:
The enthalpy of solution depends on how much solvent is used. For HCl(g) dissolving in water:

ProcessΔH (kJ mol⁻¹)
HCl + 10 aq−69.01
HCl + 25 aq−72.03
HCl + 40 aq−72.79
HCl + ∞ aq−74.85 (limiting value)

Subtracting two steps: HCl·25 aq + 15 aq → HCl·40 aq; ΔH = −72.79 − (−72.03) = −0.76 kJ mol⁻¹. This is the enthalpy of dilution: the heat change when extra solvent is added to a solution.

It depends on the original concentration and the amount of solvent added. As dilution increases, ΔH approaches the infinite-dilution value.

questions.q: ΔH for HCl(g) + 10 aq is −69.0 kJ mol⁻¹ and for HCl(g) + 20 aq is −71.0 kJ mol⁻¹. Enthalpy of dilution for HCl·10aq + 10aq → HCl·20aq is:
questions.e: Subtract: −71.0 − (−69.0) = −2.0 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.q: As more and more solvent is added, the enthalpy of solution:
questions.e: NCERT: it approaches the limiting value at infinite dilution.

children.title: 5.6 Spontaneity
children.synopsis: The First Law tracks energy but says nothing about direction. Heat flows hot → cold, gases spread out, carbon burns to CO2, and never the reverse on their own. This section asks what decides the direction of change. It tests enthalpy (not enough), then entropy (enough for isolated systems), then Gibbs energy, the working criterion at constant T and p. It ends with the Second and Third Laws.

children.title: What 'Spontaneous' Means
children.synopsis:
Spontaneous does not mean instantaneous. H2 and O2 can sit mixed at room temperature for years with no visible change. The reaction is happening, just extremely slowly, and it is still called spontaneous.

Spontaneity means 'having the potential to proceed without the assistance of an external agency'.
  • It says nothing about rate.
  • A spontaneous process cannot reverse its direction on its own. A spontaneous process is irreversible and can be reversed only by an external agency.
traps: 'Spontaneous' ≠ 'fast'. Rate is kinetics; spontaneity is thermodynamics.

questions.q: A mixture of H₂ and O₂ at room temperature shows no perceptible change for years. The reaction is:
questions.e: NCERT uses this exact example: spontaneity concerns the potential to proceed, not the rate.

questions.q: Which statement about a spontaneous process is correct?
o: It can reverse direction on its own
It is irreversible and can be reversed only by an external agency
questions.e: NCERT summary statement on spontaneous processes.

children.title: (a) Is Decrease in Enthalpy the Criterion?
children.synopsis:
Water flows downhill and stones fall, both towards lower potential energy. By analogy, perhaps reactions are spontaneous because enthalpy decreases. Many spontaneous reactions are indeed exothermic:

  • ½N2 + 3/2 H2 → NH3; ΔH = −46.1 kJ mol⁻¹
  • ½H2 + ½Cl2 → HCl; ΔH = −92.32 kJ mol⁻¹
  • H2 + ½O2 → H2O(l); ΔH = −285.8 kJ mol⁻¹

But some endothermic reactions are also spontaneous:

  • ½N2 + O2 → NO2; ΔH = +33.2 kJ mol⁻¹
  • C(graphite) + 2S(l) → CS2(l); ΔH = +128.5 kJ mol⁻¹

Conclusion: a decrease in enthalpy contributes to spontaneity but is not the criterion.

questions.q: The fact that some endothermic reactions are spontaneous shows that:
o: Enthalpy decrease is the sole criterion for spontaneity
Enthalpy decrease may contribute but is not the sole criterion
questions.e: NCERT: decrease in enthalpy may be a contributory factor but is not true for all cases.

children.title: (b) Entropy (S)
children.synopsis: When ΔH = 0 a process can still be spontaneous, so something else must drive it. That something is entropy (S).

children.title: Entropy as Disorder
children.synopsis:
Diffusion of two gases (Fig 5.11) in an isolated container has ΔH = 0, yet it is spontaneous. Before the partition is removed, you know which gas is on which side. Afterwards, a molecule you pick could be A or B: the system has become less predictable, more chaotic.

Postulate: in an isolated system, energy tends to become more disordered. This disorder is measured by entropy, S.

  • Greater disorder means higher entropy.
  • For a given substance: crystalline solid (lowest S) < liquid < gas (highest S).
  • In reactions, S changes because atoms or ions rearrange. A more disordered product structure means ΔS > 0.

Quick ΔS predictions (Problem 5.10):

  • Liquid → crystal: S decreases
  • Heating a crystal from 0 K to 115 K: S increases
  • 2NaHCO3(s) → Na2CO3(s) + CO2(g) + H2O(g): S increases (gases formed)
  • H2(g) → 2H(g): S increases (more particles)
points: S(solid) < S(liquid) < S(gas).
More gas moles or more particles means ΔS > 0.

questions.q: In which process does entropy decrease?
questions.e: Liquid → ordered solid means S decreases.

questions.q: For which reaction is ΔS positive?
questions.e: A gas forms from a solid (Δn_g = +1), so disorder increases.

questions.q: For 2Cl(g) → Cl₂(g), the signs of ΔH and ΔS are:
questions.e: Bond formation releases energy (ΔH < 0), and 2 particles → 1 lowers disorder (ΔS < 0).

children.title: ΔS = q(rev)/T and ΔS(total) > 0
children.synopsis:
Heat randomises a system. The same heat causes more disorder at a lower temperature than at a higher one, because a hot system is already chaotic. So ΔS ∝ q and ∝ 1/T:

ΔS = qrev / T (Eq. 5.18)

Entropy is a state function, so ΔS is path independent. We compute it along a reversible path.

For a spontaneous process:

ΔStotal = ΔSsystem + ΔSsurr > 0 (Eq. 5.19)

  • At equilibrium, entropy is maximum and ΔS = 0.
  • For isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, ΔU = 0 for both reversible and irreversible paths, but ΔStotal ≠ 0 for the irreversible one. ΔU cannot tell reversible from irreversible; ΔS can.

Problem 5.11: 4Fe + 3O2 → 2Fe2O3 has ΔSsys = −549.4 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, yet the reaction is spontaneous. ΔSsurr = −ΔH/T = 1648 × 10³/298 = +5530. So ΔStotal = +4980.6 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ > 0.

questions.q: ΔfusH of ice is 6.0 kJ mol⁻¹ at 273 K. The entropy of fusion is about:
questions.e: ΔS = q_rev/T = 6000/273 ≈ 22.0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

questions.q: A reaction releases 100 kJ of heat at 300 K. The entropy change of the surroundings is:
For a spontaneous process in an isolated system:

children.title: (c) Gibbs Energy & Spontaneity
children.synopsis:
Most reactions occur in closed or open systems where both H and S change, so neither alone decides spontaneity. We define the Gibbs energy:

G = H − TS (Eq. 5.20)

G is an extensive property and a state function.

children.title: Gibbs Equation: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS
children.synopsis:
ΔGsys = ΔHsys − TΔSsys − SsysΔT. At constant temperature this becomes:

ΔG = ΔH − TΔS (Eq. 5.21)

This is the Gibbs equation, 'one of the most important equations in chemistry'. It combines energy (ΔH) and disorder (ΔS) in one criterion.

Units: ΔG is an energy, since T × ΔS = K × J K⁻¹ = J.
traps: Keep units consistent. ΔS is usually in J K⁻¹ and ΔH in kJ, so convert one of them.

questions.q: Gibbs energy G is defined as:
questions.e: NCERT Eq. 5.20: G = H − TS.

questions.q: Which statement about Gibbs energy is correct?
o: It is an extensive property and a state function
It has units of J K⁻¹
questions.e: NCERT: G is extensive and a state function; its units are energy.

children.title: ΔG < 0 Means Spontaneous (Derivation)
children.synopsis:
Start from ΔStotal = ΔSsys + ΔSsurr. When the system is in thermal equilibrium with the surroundings, ΔSsurr = −ΔHsys/T.

So TΔStotal = TΔSsys − ΔHsys. A spontaneous process needs ΔStotal > 0, so ΔHsys − TΔSsys < 0, which means

ΔG = ΔH − TΔS < 0 (Eq. 5.22)

ΔGProcess
< 0Spontaneous
> 0Non-spontaneous
= 0Equilibrium

Free energy: TΔS is energy not available for useful work, so ΔG is the net energy available to do useful work. Hence the name 'free energy'.

This criterion applies at constant temperature and pressure.

questions.q: At constant T and p, a process is spontaneous if:
questions.e: ΔG < 0 corresponds to ΔS_total > 0.

questions.q: ΔG is called 'free energy' because it represents:
o: Net energy available to do useful work
questions.e: TΔS is unavailable for work; ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is the useful part.

children.title: Effect of Temperature (Table 5.4)
children.synopsis:
ΔHΔSΔGResult
−+always −Spontaneous at all T
−−− at low T, + at high TSpontaneous at low T
+++ at low T, − at high TSpontaneous at high T
+−always +Non-spontaneous at all T

When ΔH and ΔS have the same sign, temperature decides. The crossover temperature is where ΔG = 0:

T = ΔH / ΔS

For ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0, the reaction becomes spontaneous when TΔS outweighs ΔH. Either ΔS is small and T must be high, or ΔS is large and T can be modest. This is one reason reactions are often run at high temperature.

NCERT note: 'low' and 'high' T are relative. For some reactions 'high' can mean room temperature.

children.title: (d) Second Law of Thermodynamics
children.synopsis:
In an isolated system the energy stays constant, so the natural direction of spontaneous change is increasing entropy. This is the Second Law of Thermodynamics (it has several equivalent statements).

It explains why spontaneous exothermic reactions are so common: the released heat increases the disorder of the surroundings, which makes ΔStotal positive.

questions.q: The second law explains why exothermic reactions are commonly spontaneous because:
o: They decrease the entropy of surroundings
Heat released increases the entropy of the surroundings, making ΔS_total positive
They occur only in isolated systems
questions.e: NCERT: heat released raises the surroundings' disorder, so the total entropy change is positive.

children.title: (e) Third Law & Absolute Entropy
children.synopsis:
Molecules have translational (straight-line), rotational (spinning) and vibrational (bond stretching) motion. Raising T makes these motions more vigorous, so S increases. Lowering T lowers S.

The entropy of any pure crystalline substance approaches zero as the temperature approaches absolute zero.

This is the Third Law. The reason is the perfect order of a crystal at 0 K.

  • It is limited to pure crystalline solids. Solutions and supercooled liquids do not have zero entropy at 0 K.
  • Importance: it lets us calculate absolute entropies from thermal data alone, by summing qrev/T from 0 K to 298 K. Standard entropies can then be combined Hess-style.
traps: Unlike U and H, entropy HAS an absolute value, thanks to the Third Law.

questions.e: Third law of thermodynamics.

questions.q: For which of the following is the entropy NOT zero at 0 K?
questions.e: NCERT: solutions and supercooled liquids retain entropy at 0 K.

questions.q: Which thermodynamic quantity can be given an absolute value?
questions.e: The third law lets absolute entropy be calculated from thermal data.

children.title: 5.7 Gibbs Energy Change & Equilibrium
children.synopsis: ΔG predicts spontaneity and the maximum useful work obtainable. For reactions that can go both ways, it also links to the equilibrium constant K.
formulas: ΔrG° = −RT ln K = −2.303 RT log K

children.title: ΔᵣG = 0 at Equilibrium
children.synopsis:
In a reversible chemical reaction, both directions run at once and a dynamic equilibrium sets in. Both directions can't proceed with a decrease in free energy unless, at equilibrium, the free energy of the system is at a minimum. Otherwise the system would move spontaneously towards lower G.

Criterion for equilibrium (A + B ⇌ C + D): ΔrG = 0

questions.q: At equilibrium, the Gibbs energy of the system is:
questions.e: G is at a minimum at equilibrium, so Δ_rG = 0.

children.title: ΔᵣG° = −RT ln K
children.synopsis:
When all species are in their standard states:

0 = ΔrG° + RT ln K ⟹ ΔrG° = −RT ln K = −2.303 RT log K (Eq. 5.23)

Combined with ΔrG° = ΔrH° − TΔrS° (Eq. 5.24):

ΔrG°KMeaning
< 0> 1Products favoured
= 0= 1—
> 0< 1Reactants favoured
  • Strongly endothermic (large +ΔH): K ≪ 1, so little product.
  • Strongly exothermic (large −ΔH): ΔG likely large and negative, K ≫ 1, so the reaction goes nearly to completion.
  • ΔS also matters. Its sign shifts K accordingly.

Uses: (i) estimate ΔG from ΔH and ΔS, then get K at any T for economic yields; (ii) measure K in the lab, then get ΔG at other temperatures.
traps: ΔG = 0 at equilibrium, but ΔG° is generally NOT zero. ΔG° = 0 only when K = 1.
